units.title: Kinetics
units.blurb: Measure reaction rates, find rate laws, and connect them to reaction mechanisms.

units.title: Chemical Equilibrium
units.blurb: Write and use equilibrium constants, predict shifts, and solve for the amounts at equilibrium.

units.title: Acids and Bases
units.blurb: pH with logarithms, weak acids and bases, salts, buffers and titration curves.

units.title: Solubility and Complex Ions
units.blurb: Solubility products, the common-ion effect, predicting precipitates, pH effects and complex ions.

units.title: Entropy and Free Energy
units.blurb: What makes a process thermodynamically favored, and how that connects to K and to rates.

units.title: Electrochemistry
units.blurb: Galvanic and electrolytic cells, cell potentials, the Nernst equation and Faraday's law.

units.title: Nuclear Chemistry in Depth
units.blurb: Nuclear stability, binding energy and the rate of radioactive decay.

units.title: Coordination Compounds
units.blurb: Ligands, names, shapes, isomers and the colors of transition-metal complexes.

topics.title: Measuring Reaction Rates
topics.short: A rate is the change in concentration per unit time, divided by each substance's coefficient so that every substance gives the same rate.
topics.trouble: Students report a negative rate for a reactant, or forget to divide by the coefficients when they compare the rates of different substances.

topics.title: Rate Laws and Reaction Order
topics.short: rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, where the orders m and n are found by experiment.
topics.trouble: Students read the orders from the coefficients of the overall balanced equation.

topics.title: The Method of Initial Rates
topics.short: Compare experiments in which only one concentration changes to find each order, then k and its units.
topics.trouble: Students compare two experiments in which more than one concentration changed, or give k without its units.

topics.title: First-Order Reactions
topics.short: ln[A] falls in a straight line with time, and the half-life, t½ = 0.693/k, never changes.
topics.trouble: Students think a first-order half-life gets longer or shorter as the reactant runs down.

topics.title: Zero- and Second-Order Reactions
topics.short: [A] or 1/[A] changes in a straight line with time, and the half-life depends on the starting concentration.
topics.trouble: Students use the first-order half-life formula for every order.

topics.title: Finding the Order from a Graph
topics.short: Plot [A], ln[A] and 1/[A] against time; the straight one gives the order, and its slope gives k.
topics.trouble: Students pick the plot that looks steepest instead of the one that is straight, or forget that k is minus the slope for zero- and first-order plots.

topics.title: The Arrhenius Equation
topics.short: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT), so rate constants at two temperatures reveal the activation energy.
topics.trouble: Students use Celsius temperatures, or put Ea in kJ/mol beside R in J/(mol·K).

topics.title: Elementary Steps and Molecularity
topics.short: For a single elementary step, the rate law comes straight from its coefficients.
topics.trouble: Students write the rate law of an overall reaction from its coefficients as if it were one elementary step.

topics.title: Reaction Mechanisms
topics.short: The steps add up to the overall equation; intermediates are made and then used, and catalysts are used and then remade.
topics.trouble: Students mix up intermediates and catalysts.

topics.title: The Rate-Determining Step
topics.short: When the first step is slow, its rate law is the rate law of the whole reaction.
topics.trouble: Students write the rate law from a fast step, or include species that react only after the slow step.

topics.title: A Fast Equilibrium Before a Slow Step
topics.short: Set the forward and reverse rates of the fast step equal to replace an intermediate's concentration.
topics.trouble: Students leave the intermediate's concentration in the final rate law.

topics.title: Energy Profiles for Multistep Reactions
topics.short: Each step is a hump: intermediates sit in the valleys and transition states at the peaks.
topics.trouble: Students think the step with the biggest drop in energy is the slow step, or confuse an intermediate with a transition state.

topics.title: Catalysis
topics.short: Homogeneous, heterogeneous and enzyme catalysts open a new mechanism with a lower barrier.
topics.trouble: Students think a catalyst raises the amount of product at equilibrium, or that it speeds up only the forward reaction.

topics.title: The Equilibrium Constant
topics.short: K is products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient, with pure solids and liquids left out.
topics.trouble: Students put solids and pure liquids into K, or forget to raise the concentrations to their coefficients.

topics.title: What the Size of K Tells You
topics.short: A large K means mostly products at equilibrium; a small K means mostly reactants.
topics.trouble: Students think a large K means a fast reaction.

topics.title: Reversing, Scaling and Adding Reactions
topics.short: Reversing gives 1/K, multiplying by n gives Kⁿ, and adding reactions multiplies their K values.
topics.trouble: Students double K when the equation is doubled instead of squaring it, or add K values when they add reactions.

topics.title: Kp and Kc
topics.short: For gases, Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn counts only moles of gas.
topics.trouble: Students count solids and liquids in Δn, or use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) where 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) belongs.

topics.title: The Reaction Quotient
topics.short: Compare Q with K to see which way a reaction will go.
topics.trouble: Students say a reaction with Q < K shifts toward the reactants.

topics.title: Calculating K with an ICE Table
topics.short: Use the change in one amount and the coefficients to find every amount at equilibrium, then K.
topics.trouble: Students put the starting concentrations into K, or forget to scale the changes by the coefficients.

topics.title: Finding Equilibrium Concentrations
topics.short: Set up an ICE table and solve for x, using the quadratic formula when needed.
topics.trouble: Students keep the root of the quadratic that makes a concentration negative.

topics.title: The Small-x Approximation
topics.short: When K is tiny, x is small next to the starting amount; check that it is under 5%.
topics.trouble: Students drop x when K is large, or never check whether the approximation held.

topics.title: Le Chatelier's Principle with Q and K
topics.short: Changes in concentration or volume move Q away from K; only a temperature change alters K itself.
topics.trouble: Students think a concentration change alters K, or that adding an inert gas at constant volume shifts the equilibrium.

topics.title: pH of Strong Acids and Bases
topics.short: Use logarithms to find the pH and pOH of any strong acid or base solution.
topics.trouble: Students drop the minus sign in −log, or treat Ba(OH)₂ as giving one OH⁻ per formula unit instead of two.

topics.title: Acid and Base Constants
topics.short: Ka and Kb measure strength, pKa = −log Ka, and Ka × Kb = Kw for a conjugate pair.
topics.trouble: Students think a larger pKa means a stronger acid.

topics.title: pH of a Weak Acid
topics.short: Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for [H₃O⁺], then take the pH.
topics.trouble: Students treat a weak acid as fully ionized, setting [H₃O⁺] equal to the acid's concentration.

topics.title: Percent Ionization
topics.short: The share of a weak acid that ionizes grows as the solution is diluted.
topics.trouble: Students think diluting a weak acid lowers its percent ionization.

topics.title: pH of a Weak Base
topics.short: Solve Kb for [OH⁻], then change pOH to pH.
topics.trouble: Students report the pOH as the pH, or use Ka where Kb is needed.

topics.title: Acidic, Basic and Neutral Salts
topics.short: Ions from weak acids or weak bases react with water and shift the pH.
topics.trouble: Students think every salt solution is neutral because salts come from neutralization.

topics.title: Polyprotic Acids
topics.short: Each proton comes off with a much smaller Ka, so the first step sets the pH.
topics.trouble: Students add up the H₃O⁺ from every step as if each step ionized as much as the first.

topics.title: Molecular Structure and Acid Strength
topics.short: Bond strength, bond polarity and resonance in the conjugate base explain which acids are stronger.
topics.trouble: Students say HF is the strongest hydrohalic acid because fluorine is the most electronegative, missing the very strong H–F bond.

topics.title: How Buffers Work
topics.short: A weak acid and its conjugate base use up added acid or base, so the pH barely moves.
topics.trouble: Students think a buffer keeps the pH from changing at all, or that a strong acid mixed with its salt makes a buffer.

topics.title: The Henderson–Hasselbalch Equation
topics.short: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) for a buffer.
topics.trouble: Students put the acid over the base inside the log, which flips the sign of the correction.

topics.title: pH, pKa and Which Form Dominates
topics.short: Below the pKa the acid form dominates; above it the base form does.
topics.trouble: Students say the protonated form dominates when the pH is above the pKa.

topics.title: Adding Acid or Base to a Buffer
topics.short: Do the neutralization stoichiometry first, then use the new ratio in the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation.
topics.trouble: Students put the added moles into an equilibrium calculation before they do the neutralization.

topics.title: Buffer Capacity and Choosing a Buffer
topics.short: Pick an acid whose pKa is near the pH you want; more of both parts means more capacity.
topics.trouble: Students think a buffer's capacity depends only on its pH, not on how much acid and base it holds.

topics.title: Strong Acid–Strong Base Titration Curves
topics.short: Find the pH before, at and after the equivalence point.
topics.trouble: Students forget to add the two volumes together when they find concentrations after mixing.

topics.title: Weak Acid–Strong Base Titration Curves
topics.short: Halfway to equivalence the pH equals the pKa, and at equivalence the pH is above 7.
topics.trouble: Students think the equivalence point is always at pH 7.

topics.title: Choosing an Indicator
topics.short: Choose an indicator whose color change falls on the steep part of the titration curve.
topics.trouble: Students pick an indicator that changes color at pH 7 for every titration.

topics.title: The Solubility Product
topics.short: Ksp describes a slightly soluble salt in equilibrium with its ions, and gives its molar solubility.
topics.trouble: Students forget to raise an ion's concentration to its coefficient, writing Ksp = s² for PbI₂ instead of 4s³.

topics.title: Comparing Solubilities
topics.short: Ksp ranks solubility directly only for salts that release the same number of ions.
topics.trouble: Students rank salts by Ksp even when they release different numbers of ions.

topics.title: The Common-Ion Effect
topics.short: A salt dissolves less in a solution that already holds one of its ions.
topics.trouble: Students use the molar solubility in pure water even when a common ion is already present.

topics.title: Will a Precipitate Form?
topics.short: Compare Q with Ksp after mixing, remembering that mixing dilutes both solutions.
topics.trouble: Students forget that mixing two solutions dilutes both of them.

topics.title: pH and Solubility
topics.short: Salts with basic anions, such as hydroxides and carbonates, dissolve better in acid.
topics.trouble: Students expect pH to change the solubility of every salt, including those with neutral anions such as chloride.

topics.title: Lewis Acids and Complex Ions
topics.short: Metal ions accept electron pairs from ligands, and Kf measures how tightly the complex holds together.
topics.trouble: Students think a Lewis acid must contain hydrogen, or that forming a complex ion makes a salt less soluble.

topics.title: Entropy and Microstates
topics.short: Entropy counts the ways to arrange particles and energy: S = k ln W.
topics.trouble: Students think of entropy only as messiness, so they misjudge cases like two gases mixing or energy spreading out.

topics.title: Predicting the Sign of ΔS
topics.short: Entropy rises with more moles of gas, with melting, boiling and dissolving, and with warming.
topics.trouble: Students count all the moles in an equation instead of only the moles of gas.

topics.title: Absolute Entropies and ΔS°
topics.short: ΔS°(reaction) = Σ S°(products) − Σ S°(reactants), and the S° of an element is not zero.
topics.trouble: Students set the standard entropy of an element to zero, as they do for ΔH°f.

topics.title: The Second Law
topics.short: A process is favored when the entropy of the universe increases, and ΔS(surroundings) = −ΔH/T.
topics.trouble: Students judge whether a process is favored from the system's entropy alone, ignoring the surroundings.

topics.title: Gibbs Free Energy
topics.short: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and a negative ΔG means the process is thermodynamically favored.
topics.trouble: Students combine ΔH in kJ with ΔS in J/K without converting.

topics.title: Temperature and Favorability
topics.short: The signs of ΔH and ΔS decide whether heating helps, and the crossover is at T = ΔH/ΔS.
topics.trouble: Students think an endothermic reaction can never be favored at any temperature.

topics.title: Favored but Slow: Kinetic Control
topics.short: A high activation energy can keep a favored reaction from happening at a useful rate.
topics.trouble: Students think a thermodynamically favored reaction must be fast, as if ΔG set the rate.

topics.title: Free Energy and Equilibrium
topics.short: ΔG° = −RT ln K, and ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q.
topics.trouble: Students think ΔG° is zero at equilibrium, when it is ΔG that is zero.

topics.title: Coupled Reactions
topics.short: An unfavored reaction can run when it is paired with a strongly favored one, as ATP does in cells.
topics.trouble: Students think coupling changes the ΔG of the unfavored step itself, instead of making the total ΔG negative.

topics.title: Galvanic Cells
topics.short: A redox reaction split into two half-cells pushes electrons through a wire from the anode to the cathode.
topics.trouble: Students think electrons travel through the salt bridge or the solution, when ions carry the charge there.

topics.title: Standard Reduction Potentials
topics.short: E°(cell) = E°(cathode) − E°(anode), and E° is never multiplied by a coefficient.
topics.trouble: Students multiply a half-cell potential by the coefficient used to balance the electrons.

topics.title: Cell Potential, Free Energy and K
topics.short: ΔG° = −nFE°, so a positive E° means a favored reaction with K > 1.
topics.trouble: Students use the wrong n, such as the electrons in one half-reaction before the two were balanced.

topics.title: The Nernst Equation
topics.short: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q gives the cell voltage away from standard conditions, even for concentration cells.
topics.trouble: Students put the reactant concentrations on top of Q, or include solids in Q.

topics.title: Electrolytic Cells
topics.short: An outside power source drives an unfavored redox reaction.
topics.trouble: Students think the anode is negative in every cell, when it is negative in a galvanic cell and positive in an electrolytic one.

topics.title: Electrolysis Calculations
topics.short: Charge equals current times time; divide by Faraday's constant to count moles of electrons.
topics.trouble: Students forget how many electrons each ion needs, so they predict twice as much copper as can form.

topics.title: Batteries, Fuel Cells and Corrosion
topics.short: Batteries and rusting are redox reactions, and a more active metal can protect iron.
topics.trouble: Students think a battery stores electricity or electrons, instead of chemicals that react to push electrons through a circuit.

topics.title: Nuclear Stability and Decay Modes
topics.short: The neutron-to-proton ratio predicts whether a nucleus will beta decay, emit a positron, capture an electron or alpha decay.
topics.trouble: Students predict beta decay for a nucleus with too few neutrons, when it needs positron emission or electron capture.

topics.title: Mass Defect and Binding Energy
topics.short: A nucleus weighs less than its separate parts, and the missing mass times c² is its binding energy.
topics.trouble: Students think a nucleus weighs more than its separate protons and neutrons, or forget to change atomic mass units to kilograms before using E = mc².

topics.title: Radioactive Decay Rates
topics.short: Radioactive decay is first order: N = N₀e^(−kt), even between whole half-lives.
topics.trouble: Students think the half-life gets shorter as the sample shrinks, as if each nucleus carried a timer.

topics.title: Coordination Compounds
topics.short: A central metal ion, its ligands and its coordination number; find the metal's oxidation state.
topics.trouble: Students count every atom of a ligand as a bond to the metal, or ignore the ligands' charges when they find the metal's oxidation state.

topics.title: Naming Coordination Compounds
topics.short: Name the ligands in alphabetical order with prefixes, then the metal and its oxidation state.
topics.trouble: Students alphabetize ligands by their number prefixes, or forget the -ate ending for a metal in a complex anion.

topics.title: Isomers of Complexes
topics.short: Cis and trans arrangements and mirror-image pairs give complexes with the same formula but different properties.
topics.trouble: Students count rotated copies of one complex as different isomers.

topics.title: Crystal Field Theory and Color
topics.short: Ligands split the d orbitals; the size of the gap sets the color and the number of unpaired electrons.
topics.trouble: Students think a complex shows the color of the light it absorbs, when it shows the complementary color.
